title: Which of the four statements really hold?
description: Four statements about expressions are verified. A test number breaks three of them, and letters prove the one about squares of even and odd numbers. The board puts the answers back with test numbers.
teaching_notes: One idea: one example is enough to break a statement, but only letters can prove it for every number. Watch for students who test a few numbers and then call a statement correct.

source: Figure it Out (identities and patterns, question 5)
video_script.why: The child can check a simplification, but has not yet decided whether a claim about an expression holds for every number.
video_script.substitution: Multiply out each expression, break a false claim with one example, and prove a true claim with letters, as the cards in the book did.
video_script.anchor: the four statements of the book's question, each waiting for a verdict
video_script.payoff_line: Only statement three holds, and the other three do not.

final_answer.spoken: only statement three holds, and the other three do not

maths_rules: (k + 1)(k + 2) − (k + 3) = k² + 3k + 2 − k − 3 = k² + 2k − 1; k = 1 gives 2 and k = 2 gives 7
(2m)² = 4m²; (2m + 1)² = 4m² + 4m + 1 = 4m(m + 1) + 1; m(m + 1) is even, so 4m(m + 1) is a multiple of 8
(6n + 2)² = 36n² + 24n + 4; (4n + 3)² = 16n² + 24n + 9; the take away is 20n² − 5; 20n² is not a square for n = 1
check: 6² = 36 is a multiple of 4; 5² = 25 = 24 + 1 and 24 is a multiple of 8; q = 1: (3)(−1) = −3
video_script.design: One idea: one example breaks a false claim, and letters prove a true one. The two rule cards stay on the stage. The verdict on the statement about even and odd squares is left until the answer.

beats.on_screen: (i) k² + 3k + 2 - k - 3 = k² + 2k - 1; k = 1 gives 2, k = 2 gives 7. (ii) 4q² - 6q + 2q - 3 = 4q² - 4q - 3, which is odd

marks.one2: k = 1 gives 2 and k = 2 gives 7, and the statement is struck
marks.two2: the -3 is marked as not a multiple of 4, and the statement is struck

narration: <bookmark mark='one'/>Step one, statement one. Multiply out, and take away the whole of k plus three. It becomes k squared plus two k minus one.
<bookmark mark='one2'/>Try k as one, which gives two. Try k as two, which gives seven. The values change, so the statement fails.
<bookmark mark='two'/>Statement two. Multiplying out gives four q squared minus six q plus two q minus three. That is four q squared minus four q minus three.
<bookmark mark='two2'/>The first two parts are multiples of four. Minus three is not, so the statement fails.

beats.on_screen: (iv) (6n + 2)² = 36n² + 24n + 4 and (4n + 3)² = 16n² + 24n + 9; the take away is 20n² - 5; 20n² is not a square for n = 1

marks.sq: 20n² with n = 1 is 20, which is marked as not a square, and the statement is struck

beats.colours: the like terms in one colour
narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Step two, statement four. Six n plus two all squared is thirty six n squared plus twenty four n plus four.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Four n plus three all squared is sixteen n squared plus twenty four n plus nine.
<bookmark mark='take'/>Taking the second from the first, we get twenty n squared minus five.
<bookmark mark='sq'/>Adding five gives twenty n squared. With n as one, that is twenty, which is not a square number.

beats.on_screen: (iii) (2m)² = 4m². (2m + 1)² = 4m² + 4m + 1 = 4m(m + 1) + 1; m(m + 1) is even, so 4m(m + 1) is a multiple of 8

marks.even: (2m)² = 4m² is written, with 4m² marked as a multiple of 4
marks.pair: m(m + 1) is marked as even, and 4m(m + 1) as a multiple of 8

beats.colours: the multiple parts in the accent colour
narration: <bookmark mark='even'/>Step three, statement three. An even number is two m, and its square is four m squared, a multiple of four.
<bookmark mark='odd'/>An odd number is two m plus one. Its square is four m squared plus four m plus one.
<bookmark mark='fact'/>Taking out four m, that is four m times m plus one, plus one.
<bookmark mark='pair'/>M times m plus one is two numbers in a row multiplied, so it is even. Four times an even number is a multiple of eight.

beats.on_screen: Check with numbers: 6² = 36, a multiple of 4. 5² = 25 = 24 + 1, and 24 is a multiple of 8. Statement (ii) with q = 1: (3)(-1) = -3

marks.five: 5² = 25 = 24 + 1 is written, with 24 marked as a multiple of 8
marks.q: q = 1 is chosen, and (3)(-1) = -3 is written and marked as not a multiple of 4

narration: <bookmark mark='six'/>Step four, put the answers back in the question, with test numbers. Six squared is thirty six, a multiple of four.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Five squared is twenty five, which is twenty four plus one. Twenty four is a multiple of eight.
<bookmark mark='q'/>For statement two, take q as one. Three times minus one is minus three, not a multiple of four.
